claim: Zeb1 mRNA is 28-fold higher than Snail1 in P7 GNPs
source: at P7 Zeb1 mRNA was 28-fold higher than the next most abundant transcription factor, Snail1 (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a comparing EMT factor expression levels

claim: Zeb1 protein is expressed primarily in the EGL at P7 and greatly reduced at P15
source: Zeb1 protein expression confirmed our RNA analysis where it is expressed primarily in the EGL at P7 and greatly reduced at P15 (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Zeb1 is co-expressed with the proliferation marker Ki67 at P7
source: At P7, Zeb1 is co-expressed with the proliferation marker Ki67 and two markers of GNP identity Siah2, and Meis1/2, and is greatly reduced in cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitory protein p27Kip1/Cdkn1b (referred as p27 thereafter)-positive postmitotic CGNs in the inner EGL.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization

claim: Zeb1 is co-expressed with GNP identity markers Siah2 and Meis1/2 at P7
source: At P7, Zeb1 is co-expressed with the proliferation marker Ki67 and two markers of GNP identity Siah2, and Meis1/2, and is greatly reduced in cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitory protein p27Kip1/Cdkn1b (referred as p27 thereafter)-positive postmitotic CGNs in the inner EGL.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization

claim: Zeb1 expression is greatly reduced in p27-positive postmitotic CGNs in the inner EGL
source: At P7, Zeb1 is co-expressed with the proliferation marker Ki67 and two markers of GNP identity Siah2, and Meis1/2, and is greatly reduced in cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitory protein p27Kip1/Cdkn1b (referred as p27 thereafter)-positive postmitotic CGNs in the inner EGL.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing complementary expression patterns

claim: Zeb1 mRNA expression is inversely correlated with the expression of the apical-basal polarity genes Pard6a and Prkcz
source: In GNPs, Zeb1 mRNA expression was inversely correlated with the expression of the apical-basal polarity genes Pard6a and Prkcz (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1c

claim: Pard6a mRNA increases as CGN differentiation proceeds
source: Not only did Pard6a mRNA increase as CGN differentiation proceeded, but the promoter of this gene was active in individual GNPs at the border of the GZ, prior to their entry into the inner EGL (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and promoter reporter data

claim: The Pard6a promoter is active in individual GNPs at the border of the GZ, prior to their entry into the inner EGL
source: Not only did Pard6a mRNA increase as CGN differentiation proceeded, but the promoter of this gene was active in individual GNPs at the border of the GZ, prior to their entry into the inner EGL (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry in Pard6a-EGFP BAC transgenic mice shown in Figure 1d

claim: Zeb1-expressing GNPs have shorter neurites than control cells (60 ± 3 μm vs 140 ± 13 μm)
source: In contrast, Zeb1-expressing cells had short, multipolar extensions (x¯ length=140 ± 13 μm vs 60 ± 3 μm), expressed reduced p27 and sustained levels of Ki67 and Atoh1, indicating arrested maturation and proliferating, GNP-like state.
evidence: Supported by neurite length measurements in nucleofected GNPs shown in Figure 2a

claim: Zeb1-expressing cells express reduced p27 compared to control cells
source: In contrast, Zeb1-expressing cells had short, multipolar extensions (x¯ length=140 ± 13 μm vs 60 ± 3 μm), expressed reduced p27 and sustained levels of Ki67 and Atoh1, indicating arrested maturation and proliferating, GNP-like state.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Zeb1-expressing cells sustain levels of Ki67 and Atoh1
source: In contrast, Zeb1-expressing cells had short, multipolar extensions (x¯ length=140 ± 13 μm vs 60 ± 3 μm), expressed reduced p27 and sustained levels of Ki67 and Atoh1, indicating arrested maturation and proliferating, GNP-like state.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Zeb1-expressing GNPs display an apolar, isotropic f-actin distribution reminiscent of GNP morphology in vivo
source: While Zeb1-expressing GNPs were motile on time-lapse microscopy in dissociated cultures, they did not display the typical two-stroke nucleokinesis cycle used by differentiated CGNs and had an apolar, isotropic f-actin distribution reminiscent of GNP morphology in vivo (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Videos 1 and 2

claim: Zeb1-expressing GNPs do not display the typical two-stroke nucleokinesis cycle used by differentiated CGNs
source: While Zeb1-expressing GNPs were motile on time-lapse microscopy in dissociated cultures, they did not display the typical two-stroke nucleokinesis cycle used by differentiated CGNs and had an apolar, isotropic f-actin distribution reminiscent of GNP morphology in vivo (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Videos 1 and 2

claim: Zeb1-silenced cells incorporate EdU at lower rates than control cells
source: Zeb1-silenced cells incorporated EdU at lower rates than control cells.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Loss of Zeb1 function in vivo leads to an increase in Tag1 and NeuN differentiation marker gene expression at E18.5
source: Consistent with our ex vivo gene silencing results, loss of Zeb1 function in vivo leads to an increase in Tag1 and NeuN differentiation marker gene expression, indicating an increase of neuronal differentiation in the absence of Zeb1 (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry in E18.5 Zeb1 null embryos shown in Figure 2e

claim: Zeb1 gain-of-function suppresses a group of genes increasingly expressed between P0 and P15
source: Zeb1 gain-of-function suppressed a group of genes increasingly expressed between P0 and P15 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous observations that Zeb1 acts as a transcriptional repressor.
evidence: Supported by Affymetrix DNA array data shown in Figure 3b

claim: Zeb1 acts as a transcriptional repressor
source: Zeb1 gain-of-function suppressed a group of genes increasingly expressed between P0 and P15 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous observations that Zeb1 acts as a transcriptional repressor.
evidence: Inferred from gene expression profiling data and supported by prior knowledge

claim: Zeb1-repressed genes are associated with tissue morphogenesis, epithelial polarization, cell adhesion and control of cell motility
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed this group of genes to be associated with tissue morphogenesis, epithelial polarization, cell adhesion and control of cell motility.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of microarray data

claim: Key members of the apical or basolateral polarity pathways (Pard6a, Pard3a, Dlg2 and Lin7a) are among the Zeb1-repressed genes
source: Key members of the apical or basolateral polarity pathways (Pard6a Pard3a, Dlg2 and Lin7a) and Cdh1 AJ adhesion molecule were among the Zeb1-repressed genes.
evidence: Supported by microarray data analysis

claim: Cdh1 AJ adhesion molecule is among the Zeb1-repressed genes
source: Key members of the apical or basolateral polarity pathways (Pard6a Pard3a, Dlg2 and Lin7a) and Cdh1 AJ adhesion molecule were among the Zeb1-repressed genes.
evidence: Supported by microarray data analysis

claim: Various genes previously shown to be induced during EMT were enriched in Zeb1-expressing GNPs
source: In parallel, we analyzed the EMT/MET signature upon Zeb1 gain-of-function in GNPs, using a pathway-focused PCR array. Various genes previously shown to be induced during EMT were enriched in these GNPs, while a class of MET-related genes were repressed (see Tables in Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT2 Profiler PCR array data

claim: A class of MET-related genes were repressed in Zeb1-expressing GNPs
source: In parallel, we analyzed the EMT/MET signature upon Zeb1 gain-of-function in GNPs, using a pathway-focused PCR array. Various genes previously shown to be induced during EMT were enriched in these GNPs, while a class of MET-related genes were repressed (see Tables in Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT2 Profiler PCR array data

claim: The protein expression of many Zeb1 targets is mutually exclusive with Zeb1 or Ki67 in vivo
source: Not only were many of these genes increasingly expressed in the normal developmental time course (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and validated as suppressed in Zeb1-expressing GNPs (Figure 3c), the protein expression of many of them was mutually exclusive with Zeb1 or Ki67 in vivo (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3d

claim: Many of the proximal promoters of key apical-basal polarity genes (Pard6a, Pard6b, Pard3a, Pard6g) show clear Zeb1 binding peaks
source: Many of the proximal promoters of key apical-basal polarity genes (Pard6a, Pard6b, Pard3a, Pard6g) and other Zeb1-regulated genes identified in our screen (Chl1, Limk2) showed clear Zeb1 binding peaks, suggesting that they are direct targets (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data in NS5 mouse neural stem cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Zeb1 binding events are highly associated with downregulated genes
source: Computational analyses comparing the genome-wide Zeb1 binding profile to the Zeb1-regulated genes identified by expression profiling showed Zeb1 binding events are highly associated with downregulated genes (Figure 4a–c), further pointing to Zeb1 as a transcriptional repressor in neural stem/progenitor cells.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of ChIP-seq and expression profiling data shown in Figure 4a-c

claim: Strong Zeb1 binding was observed at the proximal upstream sequences of Pard6 and Pard3a genes in purified P7 GNPs
source: Strong Zeb1 binding was observed at positive control regions in the Zeb1 gene and Cdh1 gene, at the proximal upstream sequences of Pard6 and Pard3a genes and at an intronic site in the Chl1 gene.
evidence: Supported by ChIP PCR validation in purified P7 GNPs shown in Figure 4d

claim: Strong Zeb1 binding was observed at an intronic site in the Chl1 gene in purified P7 GNPs
source: Strong Zeb1 binding was observed at positive control regions in the Zeb1 gene and Cdh1 gene, at the proximal upstream sequences of Pard6 and Pard3a genes and at an intronic site in the Chl1 gene.
evidence: Supported by ChIP PCR validation in purified P7 GNPs shown in Figure 4d

claim: Restored expression of Pard6a, Pard3a, and Chl1 rescued all measured phenotypes to normal levels in CGNs in the context of Zeb1 gain-of-function
source: Restored expression of Pard6a, Pard3a, and Chl1 rescued all measured phenotypes to normal levels in CGNs. Individual introduction of each of these downstream Zeb1 targets allowed GNPs to acquire mature CGN status, characterize long neurites, expression of the p27 cell cycle inhibitor, absence of Ki67 labeling or EdU incorporation and GZ exit with subsequent migration to the IGL, even with Zeb1 gain-of-function.
evidence: Supported by functional rescue experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: Constitutively active Jam-C and Lin7a stimulated cell cycle exit, GZ exit and migration ex vivo but did not influence maturation parameters in vitro
source: Constitutively active Jam-C and the basolateral polarity protein Lin7a did not influence maturation parameters in vitro (Figure 5); however, both stimulated cell cycle exit, GZ exit and migration ex vivo (Figure 6), suggesting that they act non-cell–autonomously in the complex ex vivo environment.
evidence: Supported by in vitro and ex vivo functional assay data shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: Dlg2 stimulated cell cycle exit and p27 expression in all conditions tested but was unable to rescue neurite extension or migration ex vivo
source: Dlg2 stimulated cell cycle exit and p27 expression in all conditions tested but was unable to rescue neurite extension or migration ex vivo.
evidence: Supported by functional assay data shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: Sorl1, Bhlhe40, Nfib, and Cdk5r1 reestablished p27 expression but were insufficient to rescue other features of mature CGNs
source: Four genes, Sorl1, Bhlhe40, Nfib, and Cdk5r1, reestablished p27 expression. p27 is known for its cell cycle inhibitory and cytoskeletal regulatory properties; however, p27 expression alone in Sorl1-, Bhlhe40-, Nfib- or Cdk5r1-expressing cells was insufficient to rescue the other features of mature CGNs, such as neurite extension, loss of Ki67 labeling/EdU incorporation, or GZ exit and migration to the IGL.
evidence: Supported by functional assay data shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: Restored expression of Nfib and Flt1 enhanced neurite extension but failed to rescue the full spectrum of mature CGN features
source: Restored expression of Nfib and Flt1 enhanced neurite extension but failed to rescue the full spectrum of mature CGN features, much like the genes that stimulated p27 expression.
evidence: Supported by functional assay data shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: Cdh1, Cdk5r1 and Sorl1 were not sufficient to rescue IGL-directed migration of Zeb1 over-expressing cells in longer term ex vivo incubations
source: Additionally, longer term ex vivo incubations revealed that Cdh1, Cdk5r1 and Sorl1 were not sufficient to rescue IGL-directed migration of Zeb1 over-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by 72 hour ex vivo incubation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Bhlhe40 expression could rescue IGL-directed migration with a 72 hr ex vivo incubation
source: Interestingly, Bhlhe40 expression, a negative regulator of EMT could rescue with a 72 hr ex vivo incubation.
evidence: Supported by 72 hour ex vivo incubation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Pard6a-, Pard3a-, and Chl1-rescue restored two-stroke nucleokinesis and JAM-C adhesion levels
source: Time-lapse imaging revealed of cultured neurons revealed that Pard6a-, Pard3a-, and Chl1-rescue also restored two-stroke nucleokinesis and JAM-C adhesion levels, two cell biological outputs of the PAR complex function in maturing CGNs (Solecki et al., 2004; Famulski et al., 2010) (see Videos 3–12).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Videos 3-12

claim: Restored Pard6a and Chl1 expression did not affect the levels at which Zeb1 suppressed its target genes
source: Restored Pard6a and Chl1 expression did not affect the levels at which Zeb1 suppressed its target genes, indicating that Pard6a and Chl1 did not counteract Zeb1 at the transcriptional level or non-specifically reduce Zeb1 target repression in our assay system (Figure 7a).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7a

claim: Restored Pard6a or Chl1 expression reduced Zeb1-mediated activation of CyclinD1 and CylinD2 mRNA
source: Restored Pard6a or Chl1 expression reduced Zeb1-mediated activation of CyclinD1 and CylinD2 mRNA and Atoh1 protein levels, all of which are required to maintain GNPs in the undifferentiated state (Figure 7b and c) (Ayrault et al., 2010; Flora et al., 2009; Huard et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7b

claim: Restored Pard6a or Chl1 expression reduced Atoh1 protein levels
source: Restored Pard6a or Chl1 expression reduced Zeb1-mediated activation of CyclinD1 and CylinD2 mRNA and Atoh1 protein levels, all of which are required to maintain GNPs in the undifferentiated state (Figure 7b and c) (Ayrault et al., 2010; Flora et al., 2009; Huard et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7c

claim: GNP cultures treated with SAG displayed elevated Zeb1 protein
source: GNP cultures treated with SAG, a potent small-molecule SHH agonist, displayed not only elevated Zeb1 but also decreased Pard6a and Chl1 proteins (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 8a,b

claim: GNP cultures treated with SAG displayed decreased Pard6a and Chl1 proteins
source: GNP cultures treated with SAG, a potent small-molecule SHH agonist, displayed not only elevated Zeb1 but also decreased Pard6a and Chl1 proteins (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 8a

claim: MBs from adult Ptch1+/-, Cdkn2c-/- mice displayed high levels of Zeb1 expression
source: Unlike normal P15 cerebellum (Figure 1b), MBs from adult Ptch1+/-, Cdkn2c-/- mice displayed high levels of Zeb1 expression (Figure 8c).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8c

claim: Zeb1 expression is complementary with class III beta-tubulin/Tuj1 in MBs
source: Zeb1 expression was complementary with that of class III beta-tubulin/Tuj1, an early neuronal differentiation marker, indicating that Zeb1 expression is extinguished in both normal and tumor-derived cells proceeding toward the differentiated phenotype.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing complementary expression patterns

claim: Mouse MBs contained higher levels of Zeb1 RNA than GNPs purified at P7
source: Mouse MBs contained higher levels of Zeb1 RNA than GNPs purified at P7, the time of peak Zeb1 expression (Figure 8d).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8d

claim: Most Zeb1 targets identified in the Affymetrix Gene Chip array were expressed at lower levels in mouse MBs than in P7 GNPs, with the sole exception of Pard3a
source: Moreover, most Zeb1 targets identified in our Affymetrix Gene Chip array were expressed at lower levels in mouse MBs than in P7 GNPs, with the sole exception of Pard3a (Figure 8d).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8d

claim: ZEB1 RNA was about four times higher in the human SHH MB subgroup compared to WNT, Group3 and Group4 MBs
source: ZEB1 RNA was about four times higher in the human SHH MB subgroup compared to WNT, Group3 and Group4 MBs (Figure 8e).
evidence: Supported by analysis of human MB samples shown in Figure 8e

claim: Zeb1 silencing or increased Pard6a, Chl1 and Lin7a expression restored GZ exit and migration to the IGL to near wild-type levels in Ptch1-deficient GNPs
source: Zeb1 silencing or increased Pard6a, Chl1 and Lin7a expression restored GZ exit and migration to the IGL to near wild-type levels.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo cerebellar slice migration assay data shown in Figure 8f

claim: Zeb1 is the primary EMT factor expressed in GNPs during the early postnatal peak of neurogenesis
source: Quantitative RT-PCR revealed that Zeb1 is the primary EMT factor expressed in GNPs during the early postnatal (P) peak of neurogenesis, and that expression diminishes as GNPs exit the cell cycle to differentiate into CGNs: at P7 Zeb1 mRNA was 28-fold higher than the next most abundant transcription factor, Snail1 (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data comparing EMT factor expression

claim: Zeb1 expression diminishes as GNPs exit the cell cycle to differentiate into CGNs
source: Quantitative RT-PCR revealed that Zeb1 is the primary EMT factor expressed in GNPs during the early postnatal (P) peak of neurogenesis, and that expression diminishes as GNPs exit the cell cycle to differentiate into CGNs: at P7 Zeb1 mRNA was 28-fold higher than the next most abundant transcription factor, Snail1 (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data at multiple developmental timepoints

claim: GNPs are mesenchymal-like, as they express a high level of Zeb1 and low levels of polarity genes
source: Taken together, these results indicate that GNPs are mesenchymal-like, as they express a high level of Zeb1 and low levels of polarity genes.
evidence: Inferred from expression profiling data showing inverse correlation between Zeb1 and polarity genes

claim: Zeb1 gain-of-function arrests maturation and maintains a proliferating, GNP-like state
source: In contrast, Zeb1-expressing cells had short, multipolar extensions (x¯ length=140 ± 13 μm vs 60 ± 3 μm), expressed reduced p27 and sustained levels of Ki67 and Atoh1, indicating arrested maturation and proliferating, GNP-like state.
evidence: Supported by multiple cellular assays including neurite length, Ki67, p27, and Atoh1 expression

claim: Zeb1 is necessary and sufficient to restrict GNPs to their GZ niche
source: These observations indicate that Zeb1 inhibits differentiation of GNPs to CGNs and is necessary and sufficient to restrict GNPs to their GZ niche.
evidence: Inferred from combined gain-of-function and loss-of-function experimental results

claim: Zeb1 inhibits GNP polarization
source: They also suggest that Zeb1 inhibits GNP polarization, as neurite extension, two-stroke nucleokinesis and GZ exit depend on polarity signaling complexes in CGNs.
evidence: Inferred from functional data showing Zeb1 effects on polarization-dependent processes

claim: Zeb1 directly regulates genes expected to play a role in cell adhesion and apical-basal polarity
source: Overall, these results indicate that Zeb1 directly regulates genes expected to play a role in cell adhesion and apical-basal polarity.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-PCR validation data

claim: Pard6a, Pard3a and Chl1 are prerequisites for mature CGN characteristics
source: The broad rescue of Zeb1 gain-of-function phenotypes by the Pard6a and Pard3a polarity proteins and the Chl1 adhesion molecule demonstrates that these Zeb1-supressed targets are prerequisites for mature CGN characteristics.
evidence: Supported by functional rescue experiments showing restoration of multiple CGN features

claim: SHH maintains Zeb1 expression in GNPs
source: We found that SHH, a potent GNP mitogen, maintains Zeb1 expression.
evidence: Supported by SAG treatment experiments showing elevated Zeb1

claim: Zeb1 expression persists in MB tumor cells with persistent SHH activation
source: Moreover, Zeb1 expression persists in MB tumor cells, the transformed GNP counterpart in which SHH signaling is persistently activated.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and qRT-PCR data in mouse and human MB samples

claim: Zeb1 is functionally required downstream of SHH signaling to control GZ exit
source: Taken together, these results show that Zeb1 is functionally required downstream of SHH signaling to control GZ exit.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments in Ptch1-deficient GNPs

claim: CGN differentiation bears a remarkable similarity to mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition
source: Our findings show that CGN differentiation bears a remarkable similarity to mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including Zeb1 expression patterns, target gene regulation, and functional similarities

claim: Active polarity inhibition contributes to altered GZ exit in pediatric brain cancers
source: These results reveal unexpected parallels between neuronal differentiation and mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition and suggest that active polarity inhibition contributes to altered GZ exit in pediatric brain cancers.
evidence: Inferred from findings in MB models showing Zeb1-mediated polarity inhibition and rescue by polarity gene expression

claim: Zeb1 controls neuronal differentiation by transcriptionally repressing polarity genes in neuronal progenitors
source: We report that zinc finger and homeobox transcription factor-1 (Zeb1), a master regulator of epithelial polarity, controls neuronal differentiation by transcriptionally repressing polarity genes in neuronal progenitors.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq, expression profiling, and functional validation experiments

claim: Zeb1 inhibits polarization and retains progenitors in their germinal zone
source: Necessity-sufficiency testing and functional target screening in cerebellar granule neuron progenitors (GNPs) reveal that Zeb1 inhibits polarization and retains progenitors in their germinal zone (GZ).
evidence: Supported by gain-of-function and loss-of-function experiments in GNPs

claim: Zeb1 expression is elevated in the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) medulloblastoma subgroup originating from GNPs with persistent SHH activation
source: Zeb1 expression is elevated in the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) medulloblastoma subgroup originating from GNPs with persistent SHH activation.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in mouse and human MB samples

claim: Restored polarity signaling promotes differentiation and rescues GZ exit in Ptch1-deficient GNPs
source: Restored polarity signaling promotes differentiation and rescues GZ exit, suggesting a model for future differentiative therapies.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored GZ exit with polarity gene expression

claim: Defective neuronal polarization is proposed to underlie the pathology of some neurodevelopmental or neurodegenerative diseases
source: Indeed, defective neuronal polarization is proposed to underlie the pathology of some neurodevelopmental or neurodegenerative diseases, and restored polarity has been suggested as a potential therapeutic approach for syndromes involving perturbed polarity-linked mechanisms (May-Simera and Liu, 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Classic cell polarity signaling molecules create the cellular asymmetry required for neuronal development and circuit assembly
source: Emerging evidence suggests that classic cell polarity signaling molecules, including the Numb endocytic adaptor, the Partitioning defective (Pard) polarity complex and LKB1/SAD kinases, create the cellular asymmetry required for neuronal development and circuit assembly (Shi et al., 2003; Solecki et al., 2004; Kishi et al., 2005; Cappello et al., 2006; Rasin et al., 2007; Shelly et al., 2007; Barnes et al., 2007; Bultje et al., 2009; Hengst et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; Famulski et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior studies

claim: Zeb1 functions in many organ systems, including muscle, lymphocytes, and nervous system
source: Zeb1 functions in many organ systems, including muscle, lymphocytes, and nervous system (Takagi et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Proliferating progenitors express Zeb1 in GZs in the developing mouse brain
source: Proliferating progenitors express Zeb1 in GZs in the developing mouse brain (Darling et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Loss of Zeb1 function in the developing neocortex reduces proliferation in the VZ and SVZ
source: While loss of Zeb1 function in the developing neocortex reduces proliferation in the VZ and SVZ (Liu et al., 2008), it remains unknown how Zeb1 regulates neural progenitor populations.
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Zeb1 activates stemness pathways in immature, unpolarized epithelial cells and their transformed counterparts
source: Zeb1 activates stemness pathways in immature, unpolarized epithelial cells and their transformed counterparts (Spaderna et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: High Zeb1 expression inhibits epithelial differentiation and drives cells toward epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), while low expression allows mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET)
source: It also controls transitions in epithelial differentiation and polarity plasticity: high Zeb1 expression inhibits epithelial differentiation and drives cells toward epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), while low expression allows mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Zeb1 function in epithelial cells

claim: During EMT, Zeb1 acts as a transcriptional repressor that silences adherens junction (AJ) and apical-basal polarity genes
source: During EMT, Zeb1 acts as a transcriptional repressor that silences adherens junction (AJ) and apical-basal polarity genes (Aigner et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Zeb1 simultaneously blocks differentiation, apical-basal polarity, and junction formation of epithelial cells, locking them into the mesenchymal state
source: Thus, Zeb1 simultaneously blocks differentiation, apical-basal polarity, and junction formation of epithelial cells, locking them into the mesenchymal state.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Zeb1 function in epithelial cells

claim: EMT-like events have been observed in the transition of polarized radial glia to their delaminating progeny
source: In the developing nervous system, EMT-like events have been observed in the transition of polarized radial glia to their delaminating progeny (Rousso et al., 2012; Itoh et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Persistent Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling blocks GNP GZ exit
source: We have known for more than a decade that persistent Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling blocks GNP GZ exit, but the mechanism has remained a mystery.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: Developing CGNs provide an excellent model of the mechanisms regulating neurogenesis, neuronal differentiation, polarization linked to morphological maturation, and GZ exit
source: Developing CGNs provide an excellent model of the mechanisms regulating neurogenesis, neuronal differentiation, polarization linked to morphological maturation, and GZ exit (Hatten and Roussel, 2011; Hatten and Roussel, 2011).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Morphologically unpolarized GNPs and newly postmitotic CGNs migrate tangentially near the cerebellar surface in the external granule layer (EGL)
source: They also provide a model of migration mechanisms, since they undergo two migration phases: morphologically unpolarized GNPs and newly postmitotic CGNs migrate tangentially near the cerebellar surface in the external granule layer (EGL) while polarized CGNs migrate radially away from their GZ and cross the molecular layer (ML) to reside within the internal granule layer (IGL) (Hatten, 2002; Chédotal, 2010; Legué et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Polarized CGNs migrate radially away from their GZ and cross the molecular layer (ML) to reside within the internal granule layer (IGL)
source: They also provide a model of migration mechanisms, since they undergo two migration phases: morphologically unpolarized GNPs and newly postmitotic CGNs migrate tangentially near the cerebellar surface in the external granule layer (EGL) while polarized CGNs migrate radially away from their GZ and cross the molecular layer (ML) to reside within the internal granule layer (IGL) (Hatten, 2002; Chédotal, 2010; Legué et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Excessive or constitutive mitogenic signaling in GNPs disrupts the intricate balance of GZ exit and radial migration in cerebellar medulloblastoma (MB)
source: In cerebellar medulloblastoma (MB), excessive or constitutive mitogenic signaling in GNPs disrupts the intricate balance of GZ exit and radial migration via unknown motility mechanisms (Goodrich et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2008; Ayrault et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: The balance of EMT-like vs. MET-like processes and of proliferative vs. maturation processes may be a key developmental mechanism that, when disrupted, contributes to the pathological alteration of GZ exit in neurodevelopmental disorders and pediatric cancers
source: The balance of EMT-like vs. MET-like processes and of proliferative vs. maturation processes may be a key developmental mechanism that, when disrupted, contributes to the pathological alteration of GZ exit in neurodevelopmental disorders and pediatric cancers.
evidence: Inferred from the study findings and proposed as a general mechanism
